tagline: A winding turnpike route through farmland, river gorges and West Virginia towns
intro: The Midland Trail winds between Charleston and White Sulphur Springs on a paved, two-lane highway with some truck passing lanes. Farmland gives way to rugged river gorges along the route. West Virginia’s byways guide credits its state designation to its role in the state’s development and its cultural, natural, scenic and recreational qualities; national designation followed in June 2000. FHWA allows two hours for the drive or eight hours to visit the byway, whose route includes the mountain country of New River Gorge and Hawks Nest State Park.

Much of this West Virginia route follows the James River and Kanawha Turnpike. The turnpike carried passengers and freight between the waterways of the James and Kanawha rivers, reaching the Ohio River in 1832. Virginia envisioned the canal and turnpike together as a way to compete with northern states for western trade. Later paved and numbered US 60, the road remained a major east-west connection until I-64’s completion in 1988.

Traveling east, begin at Charleston’s State Capitol and pass through Malden, where Booker T. Washington spent his boyhood. Kanawha Falls lies downstream of Gauley Bridge, where the New and Gauley rivers form the Kanawha. At Hawks Nest, US 60 reaches a clifftop overlook of the New River. Continue through Lewisburg to White Sulphur Springs at the eastern end.
notice: Farmland and rugged river gorges alternate along the winding route.

moments.title: Kanawha Falls
moments.text: A diagonal sandstone ledge crosses the Kanawha River at Kanawha Falls, creating a 24-foot drop. The falls have blocked fish movement for more than a million years and mark the upstream limit of several species common in the Ohio River watershed. A concrete overflow dam added in 1920 diverts some water toward the generating plant at Glen Ferris. After rehabilitation began in 2010, the generating plant returned fully to operation in 2012. The falls also mark a change in how people use the river: barge navigation downstream, recreational whitewater rafting upstream.

moments.title: Hawks Nest State Park
moments.text: The clifftop overlook at Hawks Nest State Park puts the New River below US 60. The park’s original building was a Civilian Conservation Corps project and now serves as a gift shop and museum. The lodge came later, built in 1967 by The Architects Collaborative. The lodge occupies a separate site from the overlook, about a mile farther east along US 60 toward Ansted. Nearby Gauley Mountain also holds the tunnel associated with the Depression-era Hawks Nest Tunnel disaster. A state historical marker at the park commemorates workers killed by silica dust during its construction.

moments.title: The Greenbrier
moments.text: The Greenbrier’s central hotel wing opened in 1913, but visitors had been coming to the springs since 1778. The Chesapeake & Ohio Railroad’s new hotel helped turn a summer establishment into a year-round resort. A later addition concealed a different purpose: the government built an underground relocation center for Congress alongside the West Virginia Wing between 1959 and 1962. Stocked for thirty years but never used for an emergency, the bunker was decommissioned after a Washington Post report exposed it in 1992. At the spring itself, a white-columned spring house carries a green dome.
